1.goal: To open the lesson on the event that is hers, and to find out what she already knows about it.
run: Ask what she knows about the meeting in Belém, and what she would want to ask about it.
Let her answer in Portuguese if she needs to, and give the same idea back in simple English for her to repeat.
Ask her for the date of the meeting and write the answer down: the sources give only November, with no year.
exact: Opening, after the greeting: "You have an invitation. What do you already know about this meeting in Belém?"
Giving her answer back, in simple English, for her to repeat: "So: it is a meeting for teachers, in November. Say it with me — it is a meeting for teachers, in November."
The two options, if nothing comes: "Is it a meeting for teachers, or a meeting for students?"
Asking for the date: "Which days in November? Do you know yet?"
1.expected: Two or three pieces of information about the event, and at least one question of her own.
1.support: If nothing comes, offer two options and let her choose one — choosing is also answering.
1.challenge: If she answers easily, ask what she would like to get out of the three days.
1.monitoring: Whether she answers in sentences or in single words. This is the third criterion of the cycle.
1.evidence: The date of the meeting, and whether she asked anything without being prompted.
1.transition: Move on when the date is written down and she has said something about the event.

2.goal: To set the situation the whole lesson turns on: someone asks her what this meeting is.
run: Read the brief on screen with her.
Confirm two things out loud: everything at the meeting happens in English, and she has a part in it.
Ask the two questions on screen, one at a time.
exact: The two things to confirm out loud: "Everything at this meeting happens in English — the talks, the small groups, and your part too." and "They want something from you. You have a part in it."
Handing her the colleague's question: "So a colleague asks you: what is this meeting? What do you say first?"
2.expected: One sentence saying what the meeting is, in her own words.
2.support: If she reads the brief out loud instead of answering, ask the question again with the brief covered.
2.challenge: Ask what she would say second, after the first sentence.
2.monitoring: Whether the first sentence carries information or only feeling (it is very nice).
2.evidence: The first unprepared sentence of the lesson.
2.transition: Move on when she has said, in one sentence, what the meeting is.

3.goal: To predict what the invitation will say, before reading it.
run: Read the three questions out loud with her and ask for a guess on each.
Do not correct: these are hypotheses, and being wrong here costs nothing.
Do not confirm what the letter asks for — screen 5 depends on that being open.
exact: Framing the guessing, so that being wrong costs nothing: "You have not read the letter yet. Guess — you cannot be wrong here."
The two options, if she says she does not know: "Does an invitation only give you information, or does it also ask you for something?"
After each guess, without confirming: "Good. That is your guess. Let us see what the letter says."
3.expected: A guess for each of the three questions, even a short one.
3.support: If she says she does not know, offer two options and ask her to pick one.
3.challenge: Ask her which of her three guesses she is most sure about, and why.
3.monitoring: Whether she can talk about a text she has not read yet.
3.evidence: Whether prediction is available to her, or she needs the text first.
3.transition: Move on when she has committed to all three guesses.

4.goal: To read the invitation once, for the main idea and the ask.
run: Give her time to read the letter once, silently.
Ask the two questions under the letter: what the meeting is about, and what they want from her.
Do not translate. If she asks for a translation, give the English sentence she needs and let her repeat it.
exact: Instead of translating, when she asks: "In English it is — they want you to bring one experience from your school. Say it with me."
Pointing, if the ask does not come: "Look at this paragraph. What does this sentence want you to do?"
4.expected: The subject of the meeting, and the request to bring one experience.
4.support: If the ask does not come, point to the paragraph and ask what the sentence wants her to do.
4.challenge: Ask which single sentence she would keep if the letter had to fit in one line.
4.monitoring: Whether she reads for information or translates sentence by sentence.
4.evidence: First isolated measure of reading in the cycle: how much she gets from one reading.
4.transition: Move on when she has named the subject and the request.

5.goal: To separate what the letter says from what it does not say.
5.interaction: S alone, with the letter available.
run: Read the instruction on screen with her.
Open the invitation on the button if she needs it: this stage is reading for detail, and the text is support here.
Let her sort all six before you comment on any of them.
5.expected: Four it says so and two it does not say.
5.support: For a wrong one, ask her to find the line in the letter that says it. The absence is the answer.
5.challenge: Ask what else the letter leaves open that she would want to ask about.
5.monitoring: Whether she distinguishes information in the text from what she assumes.
5.evidence: Which of the two it does not say items she marks as said.
5.transition: Move on when the six are sorted and the two absences are clear.

6.goal: To notice what another person actually needs to hear about the invitation.
6.interaction: S alone, then T–S on the reason.
run: Ask her to choose the two answers that give another person the essential information.
Ask her why the other two do not, before you open the explanation.
Keep the explanation short: she is a doctor of Education, and the reason matters more to her than the rule.
exact: Asking for the reason before opening the explanation: "Why do the other two not work? What would the other person not learn?"
If she chooses the quotation from the letter: "If you read that to your colleague, what do they learn that they could not read themselves?"
6.expected: The two short summaries, not the quotation from the letter.
6.support: If she chooses the quotation, ask what the other person would learn from it that they could not read themselves.
6.challenge: Ask her to say one of the two chosen answers in her own words.
6.monitoring: Whether she can tell summarizing from reading out.
6.evidence: Whether the idea of selecting information is available to her before the speaking task.
6.transition: Move on when the two are chosen and she has said why.

7.goal: To produce whole sentences from the five beginnings, with the information given to her.
7.interaction: T gives the information, S produces the sentence.
run: Say one piece of information (November, ten minutes, one experience) and let her build the sentence.
Go through the five beginnings at least twice, in a different order the second time.
Do not correct mid-sentence: note it and give it back at stage 8.
exact: The information, one piece at a time, and nothing else: "November." · "Ten minutes." · "One experience." · "Eight countries." · "Belém."
If only a word comes back, give the first two words and stop: "It is…" / "They want…" / "My part…"
Second round, before changing the order: "Again, and this time in a different order."
7.expected: Five whole sentences, said out loud, without reading them.
7.support: If only a word comes, give the first two words of the sentence and ask again.
7.challenge: Take one beginning away and ask her to say the same idea without it.
7.monitoring: Which beginnings come out whole and which still need the frame on screen.
7.evidence: How much support the sentence still needs at this point.
7.transition: Move on when the five have been said as sentences.

8.goal: To tell a colleague about the invitation, without the letter in front of her.
run: Take the part of a colleague who knows nothing about the meeting, and let her start.
The invitation is behind the button: open it only if she stops and cannot restart.
Do not correct during the production. Record it, and note what to give back at stage 8.
exact: Opening as the colleague, so she starts: "Hi, Joice. Someone told me you are going to Belém in November. What is this meeting?"
The one question at the end, still as the colleague: "And what will you talk about?"
If she stops, the first word and nothing more: "They…" / "My…" / "It is…"
8.expected: What the meeting is, when and where it is, and what she will do there.
8.support: If she stops, give the first word of the next sentence and nothing more.
8.challenge: Ask her one question at the end, as the colleague would: and what will you talk about?
8.monitoring: Whether the date survives without the text, and whether she says what is expected of her.
8.evidence: The recording: the first extended production of the cycle.
8.transition: Move on when she has covered the four points, or has clearly finished.

9.goal: To give back two points — one that worked, one to build on — and to run the part again.
9.interaction: T–S, then S alone on the replay.
run: Write one thing that worked and one thing to build on, in the fields on screen.
Write the sentence as she said it, and then a clearer version, side by side.
Open Replay and let her tell the same thing to someone who only needs the essentials.
exact: Naming what worked, with the evidence: "This worked: you said what the meeting is and when it is, without looking at the letter."
The two versions, side by side, out loud: "You said: … A clearer way to say it is: …"
Handing over the replay: "Now the same thing, for a colleague who is already walking away. Only what they cannot do without."
9.expected: A shorter version that keeps the subject, the date and the ask.
9.support: If she repeats the long version, ask which single piece of information the other person cannot do without.
9.challenge: Ask what she would leave out if the person were already walking away.
9.monitoring: What she cuts first, and whether what stays is what matters.
9.evidence: The difference between the first version and the replay.
9.transition: Move on when the shorter version has been said once.

10.goal: To close the lesson and connect it to where she will use it.
run: Go through the list with her and let her tick what she recognizes.
Ask for the confidence scale honestly: it guides the next lesson, and it is not a test.
Read Where you would use it with her and ask for one real occasion.
exact: Asking for a real occasion: "Where will you use this? A call, a meeting, someone asking you what you are going to do?"
The occasion to offer, if nothing comes: "The meeting in Belém itself, in November. Someone there will ask you what you do."
Closing, and naming the next lesson: "Next time: two people introduce themselves to you, and you ask them a question."
10.expected: One concrete situation of her own, and roughly when it will happen.
10.support: If nothing comes, offer the meeting in November itself as the occasion.
10.challenge: Ask which phrase from today she would take to that situation.
10.monitoring: Whether the confidence she reports matches what you saw in stage 7.
10.evidence: The confidence scale, and the situation she names.
10.transition: Close the lesson and say what lesson 10 will be: two people introducing themselves, and asking them a question.
